q: Most 'multi-agent' systems in 2026 are one agent with bad prompts wearing a costume. What does that mean specifically, and what test tells you whether your design is or isn't?
answer_outline: It means: a single LLM with three different system prompts called sequentially is not multi-agent — it's one agent in three roles. Different roles share weights, training data, biases, and failure modes; you can't get capability diversity by changing the prompt. The test: if all your 'agents' use the same model, the same SDK, and the same provider, you don't have multi-agent — you have role-play. Whether that's useful is a separate question (sometimes it is, more often a single well-tuned prompt does the same thing for less cost). True multi-agent requires (a) different models for different sub-tasks, or (b) embarrassing parallelism without coordination, or (c) different trust domains (sandboxing). If your design isn't one of those, write exactly what your multi-agent system does that a single well-prompted call could not.

q: Hierarchical multi-agent has a known failure mode called 'information bottleneck at the manager.' Walk through it.
answer_outline: The manager receives the original task with full context. To delegate to a worker, it must summarize the task into instructions for that worker. The summary necessarily loses context — phrasing, edge cases, units, the user's framing. Worker A solves its sub-task using the summary, returns a result. Manager passes that result (often itself a summary) to Worker B. Worker B's sub-task is now informed by *Worker A's summary of A's solution to A's summary of the original*. Each hop loses information; errors compound. A single agent with the full conversation in context never has this problem because nothing is being summarized. The bottleneck is structural, not a prompting issue — you can't 'better-prompt' your way out of summarization losses across hops. Mitigations: keep workers reading the original input directly (skips the manager-summary step), or eliminate the manager entirely (if the workers can self-coordinate, you didn't need hierarchy).

q: After Loop 7b, you're supposed to be able to fill in: 'I'd use multi-agent for ___ specifically because ___, and I've ruled out single-agent-with-better-prompts because ___.' Why is that test so much harder than it sounds, and what makes a good answer?
answer_outline: It's hard because the natural multi-agent justifications ('this is a complex task', 'we need different perspectives', 'it scales better') are all wrong — they describe nothing concrete and are equally true of single-agent designs. A good answer names a specific capability gap or constraint that single-agent can't satisfy. Examples: 'I'd use multi-agent for legal contract review specifically because compliance requires the reviewer to be an isolated process running a different model than the drafter (auditability + independence), and I've ruled out single-agent-with-better-prompts because the auditor has to be inspectable as a separate component for SOX compliance.' Or: 'I'd use multi-agent for image-to-text-to-action pipelines specifically because the image model is GPT-4V and the action model is Claude Sonnet — capability difference, not role difference — and I've ruled out single-agent-with-better-prompts because no single model is currently strong at both.' If your blanks describe vibes, the answer is wrong; if they describe a constraint a single agent demonstrably fails, the answer is right. Most learners who do Loop 7b honestly conclude their case doesn't need multi-agent yet.
